findings.consequence: Ruling 21 splits Cleon off from the party on the landing, which means the party needs a light of its own from the moment he walks away with his. Ch9 never gives them one. There is exactly one lamp in the whole chapter and it is Cleon's: L67 'Cleon was on the stair with a lamp', L99 'the lamp went in ahead of him'. L101 then inventories what every hand is carrying through the door — box, box, flat, box — and no one has a light; L103 puts Cael through with 'the middle box on his shoulder and the satchel under it'. Ch10 opens with the party holding 'the lamp' while a second light waits ahead, and L19 calls Cleon's 'his own lamp', so two are required. As drafted, five people walk a pre-Compact gallery in the dark and arrive lit. This is small but it lands on the exact hinge the ruling was written to protect, and it is the last thing a reader sees in one chapter and the first thing in the next.

findings.gate: Shared positive voice — sentence music ('Use varied cadence'); charter §8 audio-first; residual of F-008, whose repair target asked for the ascent to be split out of the summary sentence

draft_evidence.quote: He had come up the bluff by the tier gates under a pass that was not his, as a number. Cleon had walked them up himself, ahead, with the pass in his hand and not shown, until the second gate, where a party was behind it and the keeper in the coloured coat held out a hand for it; and the keeper read it, and looked past it at the four of them with the boxes, and counted heads with the pen's end — four — and wrote the number, and waved them through without looking at a face

findings.consequence: F-008 asked for the ascent to be split out of the summary sentence and staged. It was staged but not split: the sentence beginning 'Cleon had walked them up himself' now runs 344 words to a single full stop, up from roughly 250 in r1, and carries the second gate, the third gate, Cael's five-year reversal, the old town's streets, Seln's separate route, the square avoided and the price of avoiding it. Counted by splitting L31 on sentence-final stops: four sentences of 8, 3, 20 and 344 words. Read aloud — which is how this series ships — that is close to two minutes of narration without a place to breathe, at the point where the listener most needs to hold a sequence of physical events in order. It is also the one axis on which the repair moved backwards, and it is why the staged gate reads as recovered summary rather than as the scene the packet asked for.
findings.repair_target: ch09.md L31 — two full stops, no new words. One after 'waved them through without looking at a face' (closing the second gate as its own beat), one after 'and not a lighter one' (closing the third gate and Cael's reversal), leaving Seln's route and the square as the paragraph's third movement. The clauses are already in the right order; only the punctuation is doing too much work.

concerns: Density, and where the recovered words went. The chapter is 3,932 prose words — 22 above the floor, 14.5% under the 4,600 target, with 1,352 words of unused headroom. The F-002 cut recovered 236 words and the repair spent them on the ascent (L31) and on Cael's three-age sentence (L37), which is the right order of priority. But the trim at L21 removed one of only two passages that did what the card names first — 'Treswick anatomized from inside': the bench at the stair's foot with the three walks Cael catalogues ('a stair-walk, a pass-walk, the walk of a body that had never been asked at a gate'). That was a directed cut and I directed it, so it is not a regression; but the net effect is that the city is now anatomized in one place only, L71's view from the registry yard. If planning wants any of the headroom spent, the city is where it should go, and the stair-walk catalogue is the thing to bring back at a third of its old length.

The lamp fix and the tier count are both cross-document, not per-chapter. F-014 and F-009 each touch ch09.md, ch10.md and STATE_RUNNING's 'After Chapter 9' entry. Repairing them one file at a time is how the Cleon-at-the-door seam happened in the first place. Recommend they go to planning together as one reconciliation, in the manner of rulings 20 and 21, rather than to a Ch9 repair packet on their own.

'He had wanted, at seventeen, to be looked at by it and refused to its face' (L37) is correct and should not be 'corrected'. The age attaches to the wanting, not to the outcome — the parallel with 'He had wanted, at fourteen, to be looked at by it and passed' settles the grammar — and at seventeen Cael was inside Book 6's challenge proceedings wanting exactly that. The ruling that actually refused him landed at eighteen (B6 Ch18, after the Ch14 birthday), so a later reader checking dates against events rather than against wants may flag this. Recording it so a future pass does not repair a line that is already right.

Karis is not placed in the 284th's ascent. L31 stages the second gate with 'the four of them with the boxes' counted, and L39 has her already at the counter with Cleon; the chapter never says whether she walked up with them that morning or stayed up from the day before. Nothing contradicts — the gate rule counts hands, and ch10.md L17's 'five people' coming down the gallery confirms she is with the party by the time they descend — but the r2 staging made the gate concrete enough that a reader may now ask. One clause at L31 would close it; it is not a defect and I am not raising it as one.

'A careful man' as a refrain, unchanged from r1. Eight instances ('careful man' ×7, 'careful young man' ×1) across L41–L59, roughly 600 words. It is doing real work — the clerk's care is the exposure and the machine's gap at once — but at eight it has stopped characterising him and started announcing the theme. Below every charter cap, so taste, not a finding. Two cuts would sharpen it, and the line pass is where they belong.

'"Noted," Karis said' (L17) still sits close to modern register, and ch10.md L47 now gives the same word to her again in the same position ('"Noted," Karis said, and sat down'). Across a chapter break that is a verbal tic forming rather than a character signature. Flagged for the line pass across both chapters, not for a repair packet.

The counter is still staged at one remove, from the lane, and that is still the right call. Cael cannot be at that counter; the POV holds; the clerk stepping into the yard door to make the count with his pen puts the actual turn inside Cael's sight. Recorded a second time so no repair pass 'improves' it by moving the camera indoors.
strengths: Every strength recorded in r1 survived the repair byte-for-byte. The clerk's not-asking (L45–L51) — the pen making the count 'one two three four', the eye stopping half a breath on Brom's shoulder 'because a careful man's eye goes to the thing that is carried wrong', the trouble arriving on his face, and Karis's voice coming through the door mid-argument and deciding it for him — is untouched. So is the payoff of Ch8's log at L59–L61 ('The bar had not been lifted. It had not been consulted.' … '*That's the door*, he had written. It was. It was a young man wanting an hour to end.'), the three held breaths at L53–L57, Vastin's one-word consent at L35, and the whole closing movement L91–L103. The repair pass was surgical: nine lines edited, none inserted, none deleted.

The F-010 replacement is better than what it replaced, which is rare in a repair. 'the keeper at the second gate had read it every noon for thirty years and had stopped' (L17) gives back a borrowed figure to Ch8 and plants a habit that L31 then breaks on purpose: the same keeper holds out a hand for the pass the one morning Cleon has a party behind him. A thirty-year routine and its single exception, set up and paid three paragraphs apart, doing the mechanism's work without a word of explanation.

The staged second gate (L31) answers the mechanism's own question instead of asserting it. 'Cleon had walked them up himself, ahead, with the pass in his hand and not shown' settles how a practitioner's pass travels without the practitioner — it doesn't; he carries it — and the keeper's sequence (holds out a hand, reads, looks past it, counts heads with the pen's end, writes the number, waves them through without looking at a face) is the count-rule working on bodies, which is what obligation 2 was for. The added half-line on the third gate's keeper, 'a look that priced a man who carried a box on one side of himself and knew why', prices Brom's injury with respect rather than spectacle and belongs to the reader standard as much as to the craft.

The three sentences added at L37 earn their place. 'He had wanted, at fourteen, to be looked at by it and passed. He had wanted, at seventeen, to be looked at by it and refused to its face. He stood in a lane at nineteen with a box on his shoulder and was not looked at by it at all, by a rule, on purpose' — a five-year arc in three clauses, ending on the form's own vocabulary turned back on him ('and he entered that, and did not know yet which column it went in'). It carries the chapter's irony without restating it and leaves a question open instead of closing one.

Cutting the recognition clause at L15 improved the sentence it was in. '"Fifty-two sheets." He turned round then. He looked at her — not at Cael, not at anyone else on the ring road; at her, at the flat under her arm, at her hands. "I eat at noon," Cleon said.' The look is now three named objects and a refusal to look at anything else, and the terms land straight off it. The man is read entirely from outside, which is what the packet asked for and also the better writing.

Lira's scene is more hers after the repair than before it. Removing the explanatory clause at L77 leaves 'She looked at it. He watched her look. He did not say anything, because it was hers.' — three sentences, the last of which is the whole rule of the scene, unexplained. The want then lands on behaviour at L79–L81 ('And he saw it not pull' … 'the weight did not go forward'), measured against the five years the corrected number now makes true, and she writes nothing down.

The reader standard is met without softening anything. A chapter about a nineteen-year-old being counted as labour by a system that would refuse him by name contains no profanity, no violence, no gore and no sexual content, and its moral weight comes from what people pay rather than from what they say: a promise kept at the cost of a longer walk with boxes, a Silver-tier man carrying a case up three tiers on a bad knee and saying 'Yes' before he can be asked, a young clerk who nearly does the careful thing and is not despised for failing to. This is the standard being served by the writing rather than survived by it.
